<reason>Side A (CON) ran the sharper, more progressive debate. The pressure questions were pointed and earned real answers: A3.1 forced B to define the "volunteer unit" as the family rather than the girl, and A4/A5 exploited B's abandonment of the parity argument (law firm/restaurant/club comparators from B1.4 and B2.2) after A showed secular sexed codes are being dismantled as discrimination. B's fallback — that religious institutions claim a doctrinally distinct freedom rather than parity — is coherent, but it concedes the resolution's original framing and leaves B defending a narrower claim than the one opened. B's best surviving line (parents choose all formative features of schooling; CON's position is effectively a ban) was crystallized well in the closing, but A's sex-specific-burden distinction and "who volunteers for the burden" question were never squarely neutralized. A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost, though the decisive content (A1/A2 answers and the parity retreat) was delivered before the cut. Both sides used plausible background knowledge without fake precision, and both followed the Q/A format. Overall A created more comparative pressure and made the debate easier to decide; B remained competitive but increasingly defensive after the middle rounds.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over B4.3's retreat from parity was decisive: A4.4 caught PRO abandoning the law-firm/restaurant/club comparators that anchored its opening, recharacterizing the resolution as a request for exemption from scrutiny rather than equal treatment — and B never rebuilt that bridge, while A's closing hammered the same gap.</best_rebuttal>
